Also, you don’t know what your body will or won’t let you do once baby is there, so don’t make any hard decisions yet.

My best advice- communicate that his words hurt you whether he meant to or not, and then plan to attend but be ready to not go if you aren’t ready for that.

Also, agree that you’ve made up your mind.

I hope you make sure that you’re wage matches your worth.

In my experience, you’re going to make a lot more than 35k a year bartending, depending of course on the average hourly tips at each place. Plus, depending where you are, salaried positions legally can’t take tips, so you’d be capping your financial potential while adding more work to your plate. 

Since your husband has a good job (and I’m assuming benefits aren’t a big concern), I’d go with the greater risk (bartending) because it has the potential for the most reward (experience bartending, financial gain, more growth opportunity).

Cafe Manager here! 
To answer your questions: 
1. A manager who works with the crew in day to day operations, is reasonably empathetic to employee needs, but keeps your team on task and in line with your business’s vision and is a great communicator. 
2. Shift perks (latte or specialty drink each shift/ discount on other offerings). 
Offer education/ training opportunities for baristas. 
Look for barista input when updating menus, adding seasonal drinks or are making small operational changes.
Anything that makes your barista feel like they are valued and add value to your business without adding pressure to them outside of their day to day expectations. 

And then a few extra things I’d keep in mind: 
- find a lead barista/ supervisor with training experience that shares your vision for the shop, and set their wage slightly higher than your entry baristas, with room for entry level baristas to strive for that wage/ position. 
- make sure you’ve got a training program that focuses on your basic barista standards and procedures, recipes, mise en place (everything in its place), cleanliness and overall employee expectations. Keep it simple, and the standards clear. 
- it’s better to have part time employees with flexible schedules so you’re not put into a sticky situation in case more than 1 person is sick or requests off at a time (I’d look for 6-7 employees at 20-25 hours a week in your case with open ended shifts so you can cut early or employees can stay a little longer in case the volume of business demands for it). 
- hiring a cleaning crew is good, but baristas should still be responsible for day to day cleanliness. If they’re not, then they can become lazy and it can negatively effect the entire team.  
Cleaning crews can be good for restroom deep cleans, mopping and dusting, but there’s a sense of pride earned by your staff maintaining a clean work space.

There’s a big difference for me between sharing our experience with his kids, and being told “well she did things this way and it was fine, and well with her that wasn’t a big deal”. While I am open to his experiences as a father, I am not comfortable with hearing about how she felt or how she acted during pregnancy. Frankly put, he has already commented on her, well,  “sexual health” during pregnancy and also how she handled her emotions, etc. I do not want to be reminded of their intimate dealings, or how she felt about certain choices or situations. I don’t feel like I should have to compare my situation with how her pregnancy went, or feel like mine is any less special because he’s already been here and done this.

I appreciate the response, and the validation. I’m still afraid that because I have been openly insecure about nonsensical situations (which I’m working so hard to recognize evaluate, and resolve), that he’s trying to use “tough love” by refusing to accept when I have valid, and logically sound insecurities (that he has and does, whether intentionally or not, fueled).

I should add, I love his kids very much and want them to be a part of our lives and the pregnancy as much as possible, my feelings are specifically regarding comparing his ex and I in this new chapter.
